callout: A conditional yes, in English-speaking waves, and only after Australia proves the funnel. The product travels because it has no servers and no accounts. GiftLedger, the Handbook and This Week need little more than translated strings. Each new market still needs its own holiday-date data. In New Zealand and Ireland that data is national. In the UK it is split across councils and academies, and in the US across 13,303 districts. Founder hours, not cash, grow with each market.
points: About 6 million working-parent families, a £80 fine per parent per child for term-time absence, and holiday childcare averaging £179 per child per week. It is crowded: Termy (£9.99/yr), Termify (dates for 18.7k schools), Housemait and muddl. Compete as a bundle, not as another term-date app.

The Ministry sets term dates nationally, Meta CPMs are among the lowest (about US$8.64), and house and contents insurance rose 9–10% a year. No dedicated leave planner was found. The market is small (about 400k households) and pays back its launch cost in about 13 months in the base case.
Paid ads do not pay back at the base conversion

With a 60% renewal rate, lifetime value is about A$51–65. Click-to-paid has to reach 2.5% in Australia and 3.6–5.5% elsewhere to break even, against a 1.5% base assumption. Grow with organic channels and keep ads as small tests. Assumption.

Highest willingness to pay and the most net revenue per sale, because sales tax sits on top of the price. Also the highest CPM (US$20.48), 13,303 district calendars, and crowded family-organiser competition. In the low case, adding the US and Canada lowers total contribution.
scoreNote: Each criterion is scored 1–5 by judgement from the evidence. Weights are an assumption: holiday-data feasibility 20, size 15, pain 15, language 10, competition 10, willingness to pay 10, customer-acquisition cost 10, regulatory load 10. Total out of 100.
orderNote: Germany and the Netherlands score well because their holiday data is official and open. Both need a translation and the full EU regime, and neither was modelled for revenue. No accounts, no database and cookieless analytics mean almost no personal data in the app. Buyer names and emails still arrive from the merchant of record and from support email, so you remain a controller. Under the GDPR and UK GDPR that is regular processing.

Paddle and Lemon Squeezy collect and remit US state sales tax, EU VAT, UK VAT, Canadian GST/HST and NZ GST. Lemon Squeezy is moving merchants toward Stripe Managed Payments, so plan for a possible switch.
